name: Copper and copper alloys
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists copper and bronze as corroded by benzoic acid and formic acid, and by hydrogen sulfide and carbonyl sulfide. The 2025 study states that carboxylic acids are known to corrode copper and lead.

name: Lead
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists lead among metals corroded by acetic acid. The 2025 study describes copper and lead as very sensitive to formic acid and states that carboxylic acids are known to corrode copper and lead.

name: Paper
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists paper weakening from formic acid emitted by oil-based coatings.

name: Black-and-white photographic material
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists darkening of silver particles in black and white photographs from hydrogen peroxide emitted by fresh alkyd or oil-based coatings.

name: Silver
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists silver as corroded by hydrogen sulfide and carbonyl sulfide. Silver is also one of the three metals used in the Oddy test.

name: Acetic acid
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists acetic acid as corroding lead. In the 2025 study the two materials with the largest normalized acetic acid peak areas produced the most severe lead corrosion. Lead acetates identified on lead coupons in the cellulose ether study indicate acetic acid in the test tube.

name: Benzoic acid
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists benzoic acid from degraded plasticizer from flexible PVC as corroding copper and bronze.

name: Carboxylic acids (class-level detection)
notes: Reported at class level by HS-SPME and DTD. Individual acids are named only where the paper names them.

name: Formaldehyde
notes: Detected in small amount from a hydroxypropyl cellulose sample.

name: Formic acid
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists formic acid as corroding copper and bronze and weakening paper. The 2025 study describes copper and lead as very sensitive to it.

name: Glycol derivatives
notes: The 2025 study notes that glycols can contribute to the softening of other plastic materials in their proximity.

name: Lactic acid
notes: Detected by HS-SPME and DTD in the polylactic acid filament.

name: Lactide
notes: Detected by HS-SPME and DTD in the polylactic acid filament.

name: Phthalates
notes: Esters of phthalic acid used as plasticizers.

name: Plasticizer from degraded flexible PVC
notes: CCI Technical Bulletin 32 does not name a specific plasticizer, and neither does ArtifactGuard.

name: Sulphur-containing compounds (unspecified)
notes: Reported as a compound class; the paper does not name individual sulphur compounds.

name: TCPP (phosphate flame retardant)
notes: The 2025 study notes that flame retardants have been associated with corrosive reactions involving metals.

name: 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-4-piperidinol (TMP-ol)
notes: Reported as a component of hindered amine light stabilizers such as Tinuvin 770, which the NMAI study identifies as an additive of the Terostat structural adhesive.

name: Oddy test as reported in the 2022 cellulose ether study
notes: Oven at 60 °C for 28 days with a relative humidity of 100% inside the tubes. All materials ran in duplicate and were repeated if the results differed. Coupons were evaluated visually against blank coupons and rated P, T or F.

name: Institution I procedure (2024 interlaboratory comparison)
glasswareCleaning: New glassware was used and hand washed with a 2% solution of Decon 90 in deionized water. The test tubes remained submerged in the solution for several hours, ensuring that no air bubbles were trapped in the tubes. Then rinsed in distilled water overnight and subsequently rinsed again in distilled water several more times. Finally washed with technical grade ethanol
notes: Comparative 3-in-1 Oddy test (28 days, 60 ºC); materials blind tested in duplicate.

name: Institution II procedure (2024 interlaboratory comparison)
glasswareCleaning: New glassware was used. It was rinsed with a 0.1% solution of ZVG Washing up liquid HS 50420–010 in tap water. Then rinsed again several times (until no bubbles were formed) with demineralized water, air-dried, rinsed with pure ethanol and finally air dried
notes: Comparative 3-in-1 Oddy test (28 days, 60 ºC); materials blind tested in duplicate.

name: Institution III procedure (2024 interlaboratory comparison)
vesselType: Erlenmeyer flask with ground glass lid
glasswareCleaning: New glassware was used for this experiment, all Erlenmeyer flask were rinsed with deionized water and dried in the oven overnight
notes: Comparative 3-in-1 Oddy test (28 days, 60 ºC); materials blind tested in duplicate. Institution III could not meet the recommended glassware cleaning and coupon preparation constraints because of its internal operating policy.

name: Institution IV procedure (2024 interlaboratory comparison)
glasswareCleaning: Schott glassware and caps were washed with detergent in warm water (Deconex 20 NS-x, 250 mL per 10 L water, submerged in a tub), rinsed with tap water, deionized water and MQ water. All pieces were ultrasonicated for 15 min in MQ water and dried in an oven at 110 °C for 16 hSilicone stoppers were rinsed with deionized water and left to air dry. Three incisions were cut into each stopper with a scalpel
notes: Comparative 3-in-1 Oddy test (28 days, 60 ºC); materials blind tested in duplicate.

name: Institution V procedure (2024 interlaboratory comparison)
glasswareCleaning: New glassware was used and glassware was manually cleaned with Alconox (1%) detergent. A sponge was dedicated for washing Oddy testing glassware. Glassware was rinsed with deionized water several times and finally washed with ACS acetone. All containers were air-dried completely
notes: Comparative 3-in-1 Oddy test (28 days, 60 ºC); materials blind tested in duplicate.

name: Institution VI procedure (2024 interlaboratory comparison)
glasswareCleaning: Schott glasses, caps, glass vials and silicone stoppers were left to soak in a 5% Decon 90/DI water solution for 4 h, manually washed with a clean sponge, and subsequently rinsed with DI water 3–5 timesThe Schott glasses, caps, glass vials and silicone stoppers were then wrapped in aluminum foil and placed in an oven at 105 °C to dry overnight (8 h +)
notes: Comparative 3-in-1 Oddy test (28 days, 60 ºC); materials blind tested in duplicate.

name: Institution VII procedure (2024 interlaboratory comparison)
glasswareCleaning: Standard laboratory dishwasher (with Extran AP17 liquid detergent)
notes: Comparative 3-in-1 Oddy test (28 days, 60 ºC); materials blind tested in duplicate.

name: Oddy test as reported in the 2025 mass spectrometry study (CENIM)
notes: Ratings are the visual examination of the coupons by independent expert judges from CENIM. The paper refers to the 2024 interlaboratory comparison for the procedure and does not restate temperature or duration for these tests.

name: Representative 3-in-1 Oddy protocol
notes: The interlaboratory review reports the 3-in-1 version, 60 °C and 2 g of material as common practice, and 28 days at 60 °C in Oddy's original description. Other variables are not standardized.

method: SPME–GC–MS and DART-MS on exhibit-case materials (NMAI study)
observedEffect: TMP-ol was identified as the organic component of white crystalline efflorescence on exhibited objects and as emitted by the structural adhesive used in display-case construction (Terostat MS 937 in the NMAI study; the 2025 review names Terostat-9220).

effect: The 2025 study notes, citing earlier work, that phthalates can migrate from the source and be incorporated into adjacent objects, causing plasticization or softening that can affect object integrity and have a negative visual impact.

CCI Technical Bulletin 32 lists plasticizer from degraded flexible PVC as causing stains and embrittlement in direct contact, and viscous plasticizer exudate as leaching compounds from an object's surface. The condition of the PVC is not part of this scenario.

In enclosed display cases, TMP-ol emitted by the adhesive reacted with acidic compounds from other case materials to form white crystalline deposits on exhibited objects. The NMAI study summarizes Rijksmuseum findings of such acids emitted by peroxide-cured silicone gaskets, MDF panels, UV adhesive and beeswax products. Whether acid sources are present in your case is not part of this scenario.

statement: Passing the Oddy test shows MS-35 sealing can be used in a museum setting without further consideration.
scope: as tested in the 2024 and 2025 studies
rationale: In the 2025 study MS-35 sealant passed the Oddy test but showed the largest number of phthalates in its emission profile of all ten materials analyzed. The authors conclude it must be carefully considered before use in a museum setting, an insight that would be missed without GC-MS analysis.

statement: The Terostat adhesive passed an Oddy test conducted by museum staff.
scope: as vetted by museum staff; formulation, protocol and date are not stated in the cited papers

statement: An Oddy PASS alone establishes that the Terostat adhesive is compatible with objects in a display case.
rationale: A 2025 review reports that the adhesive passed the Oddy test conducted by museum staff because it does not react corrosively with the metal substrates, yet caused significant issues in display cases: white crystalline efflorescence on objects at several institutions. The screening test did not identify the emitted compound or its reaction with acids from other materials in the case.
